articles.title: What Australia's 2026 critical minerals update means for rare earths and lithium - Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.summary: What Australia's 2026 critical minerals update means for rare earths and lithium  Benchmark Mineral Intelligence
articles.full_text: Australia has given greater priority to national security and economic resilience in an update to its critical minerals strategy, a shift from a 2023 edition that placed heavier emphasis on climate goals. It also highlights the importance of international partnerships and targets government efforts where they can have the greatest comparative advantage by expanding domestic processing and refining. The 2026 update to the Critical Minerals Strategy 2023–2030 keeps the 2030 vision and six focus areas, but critical minerals, it says, "are no longer a resources issue". It announces no new money, restating existing commitments including the AUD 17.5 billion (USD 12.3 billion) Production Tax Incentive and a AUD 5 billion (USD 3.5 billion) Critical Minerals Facility. The update was discussed by Australian mining minister Madeline King at the International Mining and Resources Conference (IMARC) in Sydney on 27–29 October, where Benchmark lithium product director Cam Perks was in attendance.

articles.title: Oil Price Forecast — Brent ($115.30) and WTI ($101.79) Rebound on Ras Tanura Claim — $120 Brent Upside - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: Oil Price Forecast — Brent ($115.30) and WTI ($101.79) Rebound on Ras Tanura Claim — $120 Brent Upside  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Brent ($115.30) Retakes $115 as US Crude Stocks Drop to 410.6M Barrels Before the Midterms — Path to $120
US crude inventories now sit 4% below the five-year average and distillates 10% below | That's TradingNEWS
Key Points
- Brent rose $1.42 to $115.30 after Houthis claimed a missile strike on Saudi Arabia’s 550,000-bpd Ras Tanura refinery.
- US crude stocks fell 1.892 million barrels to 410.6 million, 4% below the five-year average, against a build forecast.
- The Strategic Petroleum Reserve holds 282.6 million barrels, its lowest level since October 1982.
December Brent crude traded at $115.30 a barrel on Wednesday, up $1.42 or 1.25% from Tuesday’s settlement of $113.88, and December West Texas Intermediate traded at $101.79, up $1.89 or 1.89% from $99.90. The rally recovered most of Tuesday’s slide of nearly $2, when regional talks involving Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani representatives briefly eased fears of a wider Middle East war. Brent touched $115.90 in early European trading, up 1.8%, before settling into a band between $115.00 and $115.60.
Two catalysts drove the rebound. The first was geopolitical: Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had struck Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom’s largest at 550,000 barrels a day, with a ballistic missile. Saudi authorities have not confirmed any damage. The second was fundamental: the Energy Information Administration reported a 1.892 million-barrel draw in US commercial crude inventories for the week ended October 23, against expectations for a 15,000-barrel build, taking stockpiles to 410.6 million barrels, 4% below the five-year average.
The single most important date for oil is not this week’s Fed meeting. It is November 3, the US midterm elections. Reports on Wednesday said Washington has told Gulf states to prepare for renewed strikes against Iran after the vote, and President Trump said on Tuesday that the war would end on his terms and that Iran must never acquire a nuclear weapon. Traders are treating November 3 as the date the risk premium either expands sharply or collapses on a negotiated settlement.
The price structure reflects that binary. Brent has risen 19.90% over the past month and 79.26% over the past year. WTI is up 13.88% on the month and 68.30% on the year. Brent sits near its highest levels since mid-2022, and well below the all-time high of $147.50 set in July 2008. The Brent-WTI spread stands at $13.51, a wide gap that reflects Middle East supply risk concentrated in the international benchmark.
The forecast through the November 1 OPEC+ meeting and the November 3 election is a headline-driven range. The base case is Brent between $112 and $118 and WTI between $98 and $104. Confirmed damage at Ras Tanura or a US strike on Iran opens $120 Brent, 4.1% higher. A credible ceasefire proposal sends Brent back to $108, 6.3% lower. US inventories that are 4% below the five-year average on crude and 10% below on distillates provide a floor under any diplomatic sell-off.
A Three-Day Round Trip: Above $117 Monday, Down $2 Tuesday, Back to $115
Oil’s price action this week shows how much of the market is headline-driven. On Monday, Brent rallied above $117 a barrel before reversing, closing the day well below its high in a round trip that left traders whipsawed. On Tuesday, the first day of the Fed meeting, Brent fell nearly $2 to settle at $113.88 and WTI dropped to $99.90, its first close below $100 in more than a week, as diplomatic efforts in the region gained momentum.
The diplomacy that drove Tuesday’s decline was real but fragile. Iran’s Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, a day after talks with Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani representatives. Qatar and Pakistan have been mediating between the Trump administration and Tehran. Those efforts temporarily capped Brent’s upside near $115.
Wednesday’s Asian session erased most of that move on a single claim. By 01:40 GMT, Brent had climbed $1.48, or 1.3%, to $115.36. By the early European session it had reached $115.59 and WTI $101.37. At 3:35 a.m. ET, Brent traded at $115.90, up 1.8%, and WTI at $101.91, up 2.0%. By 08:58 GMT, Brent was at $115.24, up 1.2%, and WTI at $101.52, up 1.6%.
The US session added a second driver. The EIA’s 10:30 a.m. ET inventory report confirmed a crude draw for the third straight week and a sharper-than-expected decline in distillate stocks, even as gasoline inventories built. By the late morning, WTI traded at $101.79 and Brent at $115.30, holding most of the overnight gains.
The pattern explains the forecast. Brent has swung between $113.88 and $117-plus in three sessions, a range of roughly $3.50, or 3%, driven almost entirely by headlines from the Gulf rather than changes in physical supply. That volatility is likely to persist until the November 3 election resolves the central question for the market: whether the war with Iran escalates again or moves toward a settlement.
Conflicting reports on Wednesday about a new proposal to end the US-Iran conflict kept the tape choppy into the US session. Each report of progress knocks $1 to $2 off Brent within minutes; each claim of an attack adds it back. Until one of those narratives wins, traders are selling rallies above $116 and buying dips toward $113.
Ras Tanura’s 550,000 Barrels a Day: A Claim, Not Yet a Supply Loss
The Houthi claim targets the most important refining asset in Saudi Arabia. Ras Tanura processes 550,000 barrels a day, the kingdom’s largest refinery, and sits alongside the country’s biggest crude export terminal on the Gulf coast. Any confirmed damage would hit both Saudi fuel supply and, potentially, crude export logistics.
As of Wednesday morning, the attack remained a claim. Saudi authorities had not confirmed the incident or any damage, and there was no report of reduced throughput or loadings. The market added roughly $1.50 to Brent on the claim alone, which shows how little it takes to lift prices when the risk premium is already elevated.
Saudi energy infrastructure has been a repeated target this year. In March, during the first weeks of the war with Iran, drones struck the 400,000-barrel-a-day Samref refinery at the Red Sea port of Yanbu, and Brent jumped above $119 intraday. In early September, Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities injured 73 civilians and pushed Brent to $99.22, its highest since July at the time. A refinery near Abha was hit on September 8. Each incident added a few dollars that partially faded once damage assessments came in.
The difference now is the starting level. In March, Brent was climbing from below $80. In September, it was near $95. On Wednesday, the claim landed with Brent already above $113, so a confirmed outage at Ras Tanura would push prices into territory last seen in the spring, when dated Brent rose past $140 and futures tested four-year highs.
The market’s reaction function is clear. Unconfirmed claims add $1 to $2 and fade within days unless damage is verified. Confirmed damage at a facility the size of Ras Tanura would likely add $5 or more, because it would remove refined product supply at a time when global distillate stocks are already tight and US distillate inventories sit 10% below their five-year average.
The key watch item is any Saudi statement confirming or denying damage. A denial would likely knock Brent back toward $113 to $114, close to Tuesday’s settlement. Confirmation would put $120 within reach before the weekend.
November 3 Is the Market’s Risk-Premium Marker
The election calendar dominates every oil conversation this week. The war between the US and Iran started roughly eight months ago, and Wednesday’s reports that Washington has told Gulf countries to prepare for renewed strikes after the November 3 midterm elections have reset expectations. Traders now see the vote as the moment the conflict either escalates or turns toward a deal.
President Trump’s comments framed both paths. Speaking at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday, he said the conflict could be brought to a swift conclusion but stressed that any agreement must ensure Iran never possesses a nuclear weapon. That language keeps a negotiated outcome on the table while signaling that military pressure will continue if talks fail.
Diplomatic efforts are running in parallel. Qatar and Pakistan are mediating between the Trump administration and Tehran. Iran’s Security Council chief met the Supreme Leader on Tuesday after talks with regional representatives. Wednesday brought conflicting reports about a new proposal to end the conflict, which kept prices choppy into the US session.
Israel adds another variable. Markets are monitoring Israeli election results, which could change the trajectory of the conflict depending on the composition of the next government. A government more inclined to strike Iran, combined with a US push after November 3, would be the most bullish combination for crude.
The timing creates a specific trading pattern. Between now and November 3, the market is likely to hold a premium built on the probability of renewed strikes. Long positions are being carried into the vote as insurance against escalation. If the election passes and the administration pivots to a deal, that insurance premium could come out quickly, which is why the bear case targets $108 rather than a gradual decline.
The upside risk is larger in dollar terms. A renewed US campaign against Iran, especially one that triggered retaliation against Gulf energy facilities or shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, would put Brent back near the spring highs. Dated Brent passed $140 at the height of the conflict earlier this year, the highest since 2008. Futures at $115.30 sit $24.70 below that physical-market peak, and $32.20 below the 2008 record of $147.50.

articles.title: Australia revamps critical minerals strategy, targeting refining edge over China - Mining.com
articles.summary: Australia revamps critical minerals strategy, targeting refining edge over China  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Australia will refresh its critical minerals strategy to place greater emphasis on refining and processing, a senior minister said on Tuesday, as competition for investment intensifies and supply-chain concerns persist.
Resources Minister Madeleine King said the revised strategy would guide the next phase of the industry’s development, with a sharper focus on capturing “more economic and strategic value”.
“It places greater emphasis on processing and refining critical minerals. Particularly where Australia has, or can develop, a comparative advantage,” she said.
Australia is one of the world’s largest suppliers of critical minerals, including rare earths used in defence and renewable energy. However, China dominates the complex and environmentally challenging refining stage of the supply chain.
Western nations are seeking to expand their critical minerals capabilities and diversify supplies as they move to reduce reliance on China for materials essential to the energy transition and national security.
Since the government released Australia’s original critical minerals strategy in 2023, market conditions have become more difficult, competition for investment has intensified and supply-chain vulnerabilities have remained a concern, King said.
“The strategy will ensure Australia remains focused on areas where we can create the greatest long-term value,” she said, adding that growth in the sector “won’t be a solo endeavour”.
US President Donald Trump and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese signed a critical minerals agreement a year ago, targeting deposits worth $53 billion, though details on specific minerals or locations were not disclosed.
EU export push
At the International Mining and Resources Conference in Sydney on Tuesday, Angus Campbell, Australia’s ambassador to the European Union, said the new strategies could boost exports to Europe, which currently receives only a relatively small share of Australia’s critical minerals shipments.
“There’s a lot of untapped potential there,” Campbell said.
Australia has been developing a strategic reserve which it plans to make available to allies. In January, Canberra said it would prioritise antimony, gallium and rare earth elements as part of its A$1.2 billion ($842.16 million) strategic reserve.
“It’s not great piles of ore sitting somewhere in the outback,” Campbell said. “It’s much more about offtake agreements, forward contracts, demand and supply aggregation, these sorts of models.”
The EU shortlisted tungsten, rare earths and gallium for its first joint stockpile of critical minerals, three sources familiar with the matter told Reuters in May.
“We are looking with a very big interest on the critical mineral strategic reserve of Australia,” said Alberto Castronovo, Italy’s special envoy for critical raw materials.
France’s interministerial delegate for supplies of strategic minerals and metals, Benjamin Gallezot, said at the summit that Paris was seeking closer cooperation with Australia across the full critical minerals supply chain, from mining to refining.
“For example, on tungsten, we need mines, but even much more strategic today, we need refining,” Gallezot said.
He also identified rare earths and battery materials as priority areas, describing Australia and Europe as having complementary strengths in the sector.
($1 = 1.4249 Australian dollars)
(Reporting by Melanie Burton and Renju Jose in Sydney; Editing by Stephen Coates and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title: Fluor Corp among US firms vying for Kenya critical minerals project, minister says - Mining.com
articles.summary: Fluor Corp among US firms vying for Kenya critical minerals project, minister says  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Engineering giant Fluor Corp (NYSE: FLR) is among a group of mostly US investors vying to develop Kenya’s Mrima Hill critical minerals deposit, after two Chinese companies pulled out of the process, Kenya’s mining minister told Reuters on Friday.
A final decision would be announced within three weeks, he said.
Reuters is first to report Fluor Corp’s bid, the timing of the final announcement and the withdrawal of the Chinese companies — Hunan Research Institute for Nonferrous Metals and Jinan Yuxiao Group Co. Ltd.
US President Donald Trump has made securing access to critical minerals a priority of his administration, inking deals with a number of African nations as Washington looks to cut dependence on top producer China, which dominates the global supply chain and has tightened export controls in recent years.
China is also a dominant player in Africa’s mining industry.
Kenya’s mining minister Hassan Ali Joho said that five contenders had submitted tenders on October 21 for the Mrima Hill deposit in southern Kenya, around 65 kilometres (40 miles) from the port city of Mombasa. They include two US consortia, one US-affiliated consortium, an Australian consortium and a Kenyan-British joint venture.
“American entities have strongly showcased or demonstrated interest by participating in our transparent process in identifying the developer of Mrima Hill,” Joho said in an interview.
“Within the next two, three weeks we should be able to award Mrima Hills to the successful bidder.”
Joho said preliminary indicators suggested that the coastal deposit contains tens of billions of dollars’ worth of rare earth minerals and niobium, a metal used in aerospace manufacturing with deposits primarily mined in Brazil and Canada.
Chinese firms said to have submitted other bids
The two US consortia are Meridian Mineral Holdings, which includes Fluor Corp and Tetra Tech, and Frontier Minerals LLC, which includes rare earths startup ReElement Technologies. Joho also said a US-affiliated consortium called Mrima Earth was on the shortlist, led by Critical Metals Corp, which is pursuing the Tanbreez rare earth project in Greenland.
A Kenyan-British joint venture called Gem of Dreams also submitted a tender, as has Australia’s RareX in a tie-up with Iluka Resources. Rare X announced in July that it had been shortlisted to compete for the project.
Fluor Corp previously built the Eneabba rare earths refinery in Western Australia for Iluka Resources, but the two are now aggressively competing for the Mrima Hill project.
A representative for the Australian joint venture told Reuters that Fluor Corp was not licensed to use any of the intellectual property concerning the Eneabba plant.
“Should Fluor make use or appear to be making use of Iluka’s IP in designing and constructing a processing plant for Mrima Hill, there would be a high chance of legal action to protect IP rights,” the representative said.
Fluor Corp and Meridian did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for a response to the Australian consortium’s comment.
‘No pressure’ from Washington or Beijing
The other three consortia and the Chinese companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the Mrima Hill project.
Joho said he did not know the reason for the Chinese firms’ withdrawal, adding that the Kenyan government did not directly engage with the bidders.
“We haven’t had any conversation with anybody and we haven’t offered any alternative to anybody… We want a transparent process,” he said.
Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters that the Chinese firms had bid for other state mining projects in Kenya on the same day that the Mrima Hill tender was due last week. It was not immediately clear which projects received bids but both sources said four other tenders for coltan, manganese, copper and chromite projects were due that day.
Joho told Reuters that one of the Chinese companies did file a bid for another project the same day, but declined to elaborate, saying it would compromise the process.
He said Kenya had faced “no pressure” from either Beijing or Washington on the issue.
“I don’t think it is in the place of anybody to tell us on how and who to work with. Our decisions purely are informed on the interest of this country.”
Shift to domestic processing
African nations have pushed in recent years to process more of the minerals they produce domestically, marking a shift toward keeping more value on the continent.
Kenya’s President William Ruto told Reuters in June that his government was close to signing a critical minerals deal with the United States, under which Nairobi would process its own resources domestically.
Officials in the Trump administration have also said the US intends to help Kenya develop a critical minerals processing industry.
A US State Department spokesperson told Reuters that US companies had proven track records and a commitment to local processing.
“The US Government will take every opportunity to help American businesses invest in emerging sectors and developing economies, including the mining sector,” the spokesperson said.
Ruto has previously said that Kenya would not choose between Washington and Beijing, but instead pursue multiple partnerships aligned with its own economic priorities.
In addition to rare earths and niobium, Kenya is also believed to have large untapped deposits of lithium, graphite, copper and nickel.
(Reporting by Ammu Kannampilly; Additional reporting by Amy Lv in Shanghai; editing by Silvia Aloisi and Susan Fenton)

articles.title: Critical Minerals: Building India-GCC Clean Energy Ties | GHT Ep.9 - Centre for Public Policy Research (CPPR)
articles.summary: Critical Minerals: Building India-GCC Clean Energy Ties | GHT Ep.9  Centre for Public Policy Research (CPPR)
articles.full_text:
| Event Start Date: October 29, 2026 | Event End Date: October 29, 2026 | Event Venue: YouTube | 
Critical minerals are becoming increasingly important to global economic competitiveness, energy security and technological advancement. Minerals such as lithium, cobalt, copper, nickel and rare earth elements are essential for renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles, battery storage and advanced manufacturing. As countries accelerate their energy transitions and seek to diversify their supply chains, access to these resources has emerged as a strategic priority. For India and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, this presents an opportunity to expand a longstanding partnership centred on hydrocarbons, trade, investment and energy security towards cooperation in critical minerals and clean energy technologies.
India’s growing demand for critical minerals is closely linked to its renewable energy ambitions, electric mobility, advanced manufacturing and broader objectives of technological self-reliance. The National Critical Minerals Mission, launched in January 2025 with an outlay of ₹34,300 crore over seven years, identifies international partnerships as an important mechanism for securing reliable and diversified mineral supply chains. GCC countries, meanwhile, are pursuing economic diversification strategies that increasingly emphasise mining, mineral processing, international resource investments and the development of downstream industries. Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 identifies mining as a key pillar of economic diversification, while the UAE is leveraging its financial and logistical capabilities to strengthen its position in global critical minerals supply chains.
Recent developments indicate growing momentum in India-GCC cooperation in this sector. India signed an agreement with the UAE in September 2024 to strengthen critical minerals supply chains and an agreement with Saudi Arabia in February 2025 covering joint exploration and technology transfer. Partnerships involving Indian companies and GCC-based investors also offer opportunities in battery recycling, mineral processing and investments in overseas mining projects. These initiatives reflect the potential to combine India’s technical expertise, industrial capabilities and mineral-processing requirements with GCC capital, international investment networks and emerging mining ecosystems.
Beyond bilateral cooperation, India and GCC countries could explore opportunities for joint investments in mineral-rich third countries, particularly in Africa, where access to resources can support diversified supply chains. Such partnerships could combine GCC investment capacity with India’s technical and industrial capabilities while supporting local value addition in resource-producing countries. Regional connectivity initiatives, including the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC), may also provide opportunities to strengthen logistics, trade facilitation and the movement of critical minerals across international markets.
However, building reliable critical minerals partnerships requires more than securing access to raw materials. Cooperation must also address mineral processing, recycling, technology transfer, investment risks, regulatory coordination and responsible sourcing. Environmental sustainability, social safeguards, transparent supply chains and community engagement will be essential to ensuring that these partnerships deliver long-term benefits. India and the GCC can therefore explore a broader framework that connects resource access with research, industrial development, sustainable mining and the development of resilient mineral value chains.
The webinar will examine how India and GCC countries can deepen cooperation in critical minerals as part of their evolving economic and strategic partnership. It will explore the role of bilateral agreements, investment partnerships, technology transfer, third-country collaboration and regulatory coordination in strengthening supply chain resilience and supporting the clean energy transition.

articles.title: [SMM Cobalt-Lithium Morning Meeting Summary] Raw material prices pull back significantly, supply-demand looseness intensifies, and the industry chain is under pressure. - Shanghai Metals Market
articles.summary: [SMM Cobalt-Lithium Morning Meeting Summary] Raw material prices pull back significantly, supply-demand looseness intensifies, and the industry chain is under pressure.  Shanghai Metals Market
articles.full_text:
Lithium ore: 
This week, the lithium ore market continued to consolidate on a subdued note.
Affected by falling lithium carbonate prices and expectations of ample supply in the long term, ore-side offer prices shifted lower, though the pace of price adjustments between ore and lithium chemicals still diverged to some extent.
On the supply side, earlier shipments of ex-China lithium ore continued to arrive, with Australian and African resources landing at ports.
Inventory at China ports and in trading channels maintained an accumulation trend, and spot cargo available for sale increased, gradually revealing supply pressure on the ore side.
Among these, the recovery of lithium ore logistics in Zimbabwe and expectations of capacity release at ex-China mines further reinforced market judgment of subsequent supply growth.
On the demand side, downstream LFP and battery cell production schedule growth slowed down.
Combined with persistently weak lithium carbonate prices, lithium chemical plants turned cautious in raw material purchasing and price fixing, with overall buying still dominated by restocking for immediate needs.
Notably, although China lithium ore inventory continued to increase, some Australian ore spot resources remained highly concentrated, and ore-side willingness to hold prices firm persisted.
Processing margins at lithium chemical plants using externally purchased ore did not improve significantly as ore prices pulled back.
Overall, the current lithium ore market presents a combination of strengthening ample-supply expectations, weak downstream purchasing, and poor transmission of ore-to-chemical margins.
Ore prices are expected to consolidate on a subdued note in the short term, following lithium carbonate, but the extent of adjustment may be relatively limited.
Going forward, focus on actual arrivals of ex-China resources, inventory destocking at ports and in trading channels, and the impact of downstream production schedule changes on raw material purchasing.

Lithium carbonate: 
This week, in the spot market, the SMM average spot price of battery-grade lithium carbonate was 96,100 yuan/mt on Thursday, down 900 yuan/mt from last Friday's average of 97,000 yuan/mt, a weekly decline of 0.9%. During the week, spot quotes rose slightly for three consecutive days from Monday to Wednesday, briefly rebounding to 100,050 yuan/mt on Wednesday, before falling 3,950 yuan/mt in a single day on Thursday, erasing all weekly gains. In the futures market, the most-traded lithium carbonate contract opened lower and moved lower on Thursday, with losses widening in the afternoon. It closed down 8.4% at 88,360 yuan/mt, breaking below the 90,000 yuan/mt level, down 6.18% WoW from last Thursday.
On the supply side, China lithium carbonate production continued to increase this week, with a larger gain. By raw material, spodumene-based production posted a relatively large increase as lithium ore arrivals combined with new production line ramp-up; lepidolite-based production edged up; salt lake and residue-based lithium production edged down WoW; recycling-based production continued to decline due to maintenance at enterprises, strong sentiment among grinding enterprises to hold back from selling and hold prices firm on cost considerations, widespread difficulty among downstream hydrometallurgical enterprises in purchasing LFP black mass, seasonal production cuts at some enterprises purchasing brine-based lithium extraction lines, and overly mediocre nickel-cobalt demand for ternary black mass, which lowered purchase willingness at hydrometallurgical enterprises.
Demand side, based on actual market transactions and inventory conditions, upstream lithium chemical plants continued to mainly ship under long-term contracts, with low willingness to sell spot orders. With production increasing while shipments remained low, inventory at this stage continued to accumulate. Downstream material plants and battery cell manufacturers saw weakening lithium carbonate demand due to declining orders, mainly drawing down long-term contracts and customer-supplied material while actively controlling inventory. Their intended purchase prices were low, and spot purchases were limited to rigid demand only. This week, inventory at this stage continued to decline. Overall, destocking continued this week, but the pace slowed. This week, lithium carbonate inventory stood at 128,385 mt, down 1,894 mt WoW.
This week, futures fell sharply again. Spot prices were relatively resilient but also dropped significantly on Thursday, intensifying market pessimism. Supply-side production growth expanded, while demand-side orders declined, downstream players actively controlled inventory, and intended purchase prices were low, further reinforcing the loose supply-demand balance. Although total inventory continued to destock, the pace slowed, and structurally, smelter inventory kept building up, with upstream selling pressure accumulating. In the short term, the weak price trend is unlikely to change, and next week's trading range is expected to be 80,000-105,000 yuan/mt.
Lithium hydroxide:
This week, lithium hydroxide prices continued their WoW downward trend, mainly dragged by weak lithium market sentiment and a pullback in ternary demand.Downstream ternary cathode material production showed a declining trend both this month and next, with very limited spot procurement demand from ternary cathode material enterprises. Some lithium chemical plants, facing insufficient downstream cargo pick-up and mounting sales pressure, are currently selling spot orders at discounts. Traders showed strong willingness to sell, with quotes basically at a discount of 7,000-9,000 yuan/mt to the lithium carbonate 2701 contract, and some transactions occurred amid the continued decline in lithium prices. In the short term, both upstream and downstream lithium hydroxide output fell short of expectations, and combined with supply-side resource disruptions, prices are expected to consolidate at lows.
Refined cobalt:
This week, the refined cobalt market returned to a rapid decline, with electronic trading prices falling from around 230,000 yuan/mt at the start of the week to around 200,000 yuan/mt, failing to sustain last week's stabilization.Breaking down this round of declines, the drivers differed between the first and second half of the week: At the start of the week, as refined cobalt spot prices were relatively high, some traders purchased low-priced cobalt sulphate from the market and sent it to smelters for toll processing into refined cobalt for arbitrage, with the hidden supply increase weighing on futures. As prices fell rapidly mid-week, this arbitrage window closed. Entering the second half of the week, the decline was driven more by capital and sentiment factors—ex-China refined cobalt and cobalt intermediate product prices continued to fall, further denting market confidence. On the supply side, mainstream smelters maintained their Ex-works price at 235,000 yuan/mt without adjustment, while other smelters continued to suspend quotes. Basis quotes in the trading segment showed no significant changes. Demand side, the previous mediocrity continued, with downstream enterprises maintaining just-in-time procurement. Notably, prices have now approached the "psychological bottom" of 200,000 yuan/mt that downstream enterprises had previously expected, and the validity of this level will be directly tested by the market going forward.
Intermediate products: 
This week, the cobalt intermediate products market continued its narrow adjustment, with some noteworthy changes emerging in quotations.Supply side, miners showed some flexibility in their offers: mainstream quotations from domestic miners have been adjusted to $12/lb, with lower offers around $11.5/lb, and prices for slightly lower-quality material even lower; overseas miners still hope to maintain quotations above $12.5/lb, but against the backdrop of continued adjustments in cobalt salt and refined cobalt prices, the difficulty of maintaining this quotation level has increased. Demand side, smelters' willingness to purchase remained subdued. Based on current cobalt salt and refined cobalt price levels, downstream enterprises would need raw material purchase prices near $10/lb to avoid losses in immediate production, which also determines that a certain gap remains between downstream psychological price levels and miner quotations. articles.title: Critical minerals getting harder to mine as deposits age: EY - Mining.com

articles.full_text:
Critical minerals are becoming harder to extract as aging deposits, declining ore grades and increasingly complex operations threaten the mining industry’s ability to maintain production, according to a new EY report.
The Top 10 Business Risks and Opportunities in Mining and Metals report ranks operational complexity as the industry’s biggest risk for 2027, followed by capital availability, supply chain disruptions, rising costs and geopolitics. The findings are based on a survey of 400 senior mining and metals executives worldwide.
“Mining has always been complex, but the degree of operational complexity is increasing as mines age and reserves are depleted and the new ones are more difficult to mine and process,” EY’s global mining and metals leader, Paul Mitchell, said in a statement.
The challenges carry particular significance for critical minerals, which governments increasingly consider essential to industrial development and secure supply chains. Producers face the task of replacing depleted reserves while navigating more demanding extraction conditions, financing constraints and shifting government policies.
Depleting deposits
Regulatory compliance delays emerged as the leading contributor to operational complexity, followed by variability in reserve grades, cited by 29% of respondents. Labour availability, material handling, processing capacity, transport and equipment reliability each affected 24% to 26% of executives surveyed.
As mines mature, operators have fewer options to adjust production schedules, blend ore or redirect material through processing facilities. Lower flexibility makes it harder to absorb disruptions, potentially increasing costs and limiting output.
Developing replacement deposits presents additional challenges as companies confront more difficult mining and processing conditions.
Capital, the second-ranked risk, is also becoming harder to secure on favourable terms. Although funding remains available, investors are increasingly selective as commodity prices diverge, forcing miners to reconsider how they finance new developments and sustain existing operations.
The survey found 44% of companies are pursuing capital from original equipment manufacturers, while 39% are seeking sovereign wealth funds and another 39% are targeting government investment.
“Access to diverse funding sources will be critical as companies seek to preserve flexibility when market conditions change,” Mitchell said.
Supply chain disruptions, ranked third, are adding pressure by affecting the delivery of mining inputs, processing operations and access to markets.
To reduce their exposure, 53% of miners are investing in technology to improve supply chain visibility, while 52% are increasing inventories or stockpiles to protect operations against interruptions.
Rising costs present another obstacle. Even stronger prices for some commodities have not fully offset more expensive inputs and the additional demands of operating increasingly complicated mines.
“Productivity initiatives are often undermined by organizational silos and deliver greater value when managed across the entire value chain rather than through isolated cost-reduction programs,” Mitchell said.
Strategic supply pressures
Governments are stepping up efforts to secure critical mineral supplies, adding a geopolitical dimension to the industry’s operational and financial challenges.
Public financing commitments for critical minerals more than quadrupled between 2023 and 2025 to about $65 billion, according to EY. The survey also found 28% of mining executives expect direct government investment over the next 12 months.
“Governments increasingly view secure mineral supply as a strategic priority and are introducing incentives to encourage domestic mining, processing and refining,” Mitchell said.
The growing role of governments could create new financing opportunities for developers, although changing trade relationships, industrial policies and investment conditions may complicate long-term planning.
Geopolitics ranked fifth among the industry’s risks, but its influence extends into capital allocation, supply chains and decisions about where companies develop new projects.
Mitchell warned that uncertainty would persist beyond near-term political events, including the US midterm elections, requiring miners to build more flexibility into their investment strategies.
Technology could help producers overcome some of these constraints through artificial intelligence, automation and improved processing efficiency. However, greater digital connectivity is exposing mining operations to additional security threats.
Cybersecurity entered EY’s top 10 risks for 2027, with the firm’s research finding 67% of mining and metals assets fall into a vulnerability zone characterized by below-average visibility and cybersecurity controls.
Carbon, sustainability, changing business models and licence to operate completed the ranking.
For critical minerals producers, the findings point to a growing tension between governments’ ambitions to secure mineral supplies and the industry’s ability to develop and operate increasingly challenging deposits.
“The important thing is not to wait for this uncertainty to disappear – it won’t,” Mitchell said. “Instead, mining companies must reassess the assumptions underpinning strategies, portfolios and capital decisions and build greater flexibility into how they operate.”

articles.title: Global trade tensions rise as EU prepares full enforcement of carbon border tax - The Herald Insight
articles.summary: Global trade tensions rise as EU prepares full enforcement of carbon border tax  The Herald Insight
articles.full_text:
In late September, global trade tensions escalated sharply as the European Union finalized administrative frameworks for the comprehensive enforcement of its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
The landmark environmental tariff, designed to prevent domestic industries from facing unfair competition from overseas manufacturers with weaker climate regulations, has sparked intense debates among key industrial exporters across Asia, the Americas, and Africa.
As the global transition toward decarbonization accelerates, the policy represents one of the most ambitious and controversial climate trade measures in modern history.
According to policy briefings released by the European Commission, the mechanism requires foreign exporters shipping energy-intensive commodities—including steel, aluminum, cement, fertilizers, hydrogen, and electricity—into the European single market to purchase digital certificates reflecting the embedded carbon emitted during manufacturing.
The European Commission stated that the primary objective is to eliminate "carbon leakage," an economic phenomenon where corporations relocate production to jurisdictions with lax ecological standards rather than investing in clean technologies.
European officials emphasized that the tariff mirrors the internal carbon costs paid by domestic European factories under the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS), thereby establishing a level playing field for industrial production.
Data compiled by the World Trade Organization (WTO) and the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) indicated that the border levy will immediately impact billions of dollars in annual global commerce.
Economic models published by UNCTAD project that developing economies heavily reliant on basic materials exports could face an overall reduction in trade value of 1.4 percent to 2.4 percent once financial assessments are fully implemented.
Furthermore, developing states emphasized that over 65 percent of their heavy manufacturing plants currently lack the financial resources or domestic renewable energy grids needed to reduce their production emissions rapidly.
For many emerging markets, transitioning traditional blast furnaces to green hydrogen facilities demands massive capital investments that local banking sectors cannot independently sustain.
Global trade representatives and legal scholars have expressed concerns that the unilateral mechanism threatens to fracture multilateral commerce and undermine existing international cooperation frameworks.
"While reducing atmospheric greenhouse gases is an essential global priority, placing border tariffs on developing nations without providing accessible technological transfers risks turning climate action into green protectionism," argued Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, Director-General of the World Trade Organization.
Several exporting governments expressed concerns that the administrative burden of calculating verified emission metrics will disproportionately affect small and medium-sized enterprises that lack specialized environmental accounting software, third-party validation agencies, and expensive compliance infrastructure.
In response to international criticism, the European Union announced plans to establish technical consultation offices and provide transitional technical aid to assist trading partners in establishing recognized national monitoring and verification systems.
European climate negotiators also reiterated that they will directly deduct any verified carbon prices manufacturers have already paid in their home countries from their final European import obligations, encouraging other nations to establish domestic carbon pricing markets.
European authorities maintained that the ultimate purpose of the regulation is not to generate tax revenue, but rather to inspire global trading partners to implement their own domestic emissions reductions and emission trading systems.
Major trading partners, including India, China, Brazil, and South Korea, have expressed varied strategies for addressing the regulation.
While some nations have threatened to file formal disputes before the WTO dispute settlement body, others are actively upgrading their domestic emissions tracking registries to minimize cross-border penalties.
Industrial chambers across several manufacturing centers warned that if more advanced economies introduce similar border adjustment measures without standardized international guidelines, global supply chains could fragment into isolated regional regulatory blocs.
Economic analysts concluded that the dispute highlights the delicate balance between aggressive environmental stewardship and international trade equity.
Setting rigorous climate standards is crucial to preventing catastrophic global warming, but imposing stringent trade requirements without equitable support risks widening the economic divide between developed and developing nations.
As global climate summits approach, sovereign governments and multilateral bodies face growing pressure to harmonize regional carbon pricing standards and avoid escalating commercial disputes while pursuing collective net-zero emissions targets.

By Olesya Astakhova and Ahmad Ghaddar
MOSCOW/LONDON, Oct 27 - OPEC+ oil-producing countries are likely to keep their December oil output targets steady on Sunday, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters, in line with expectations that further output policy adjustments are unlikely until next year.
The online meeting of seven core OPEC+ members — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman — comes as Gulf members have been boosting exports that have been disrupted for months by the Iran war. Most, however, are still pumping well below their output targets.
All three people declined to be named and said no final decision had been made.
OPEC+ comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies including Russia. OPEC and authorities in Russia did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
In September, OPEC+ completed the phased rollback of a 1.65 million-barrel-per-day supply cut first agreed in 2023. Disruption caused by the Iran war has meant Gulf producers are falling below their quotas.
Reuters reported in July that OPEC+ was likely to make no changes to its targets during the fourth quarter as it turns its focus to 2027 quota negotiations.
The group still has one more layer of production cuts of about 2 million bpd covering most members through the end of 2026.
OPEC+ needs to finalise a review of members' production capacity before setting the 2027 baselines that will determine future quotas and shape plans to unwind those cuts, sources have said.

articles.title: Critical Minerals Supply Chains Enter a New Phase of Global Competition - Kalkine
articles.summary: Critical Minerals Supply Chains Enter a New Phase of Global Competition  Kalkine

Highlights
- The IEA expects critical-mineral demand to nearly double by 2040 under stated policies.
- Lithium demand is projected to grow more than threefold by 2040.
- Copper demand is projected to increase by about seven million tonnes.
- Announced projects have narrowed the projected copper supply gap.
- Refining and processing capacity remain less diversified than mining capacity.
- Trade and industrial policies increasingly influence supply-chain investment.
The global competition for critical minerals is shifting from the discovery of deposits to the ability to process materials into products that manufacturers can use. Copper, lithium, nickel and rare earths are central to electricity networks, batteries, digital infrastructure and industrial technology. Demand is expected to expand over the coming decades, but new mines alone cannot guarantee reliable supply. The International Energy Agency’s 2026 critical-minerals outlook highlights the growing importance of refining, manufacturing and policy decisions.
Latest Policy Moves Put Supply Security Back in Focus
On 23 October 2026, the United States designated helium a critical material, citing its role in semiconductor manufacturing and exposure to international supply disruptions. The move illustrates how industrial security now extends beyond battery minerals to specialist inputs used in electronics, medical equipment and energy technology. Meanwhile, 26 October metals-market reporting showed zinc reaching a two-week high as tight inventories supported prices, even as copper faced pressure from rising exchange stocks and demand concerns. These contrasting developments reinforce the importance of distinguishing short-term price moves from the longer-term concentration of processing and supply chains.
Electrification Drives the Long-Term Demand Story
Under the IEA’s stated-policy scenario, aggregate demand for critical minerals almost doubles by 2040. Lithium is projected to record the strongest increase, with demand rising more than threefold. Nickel, graphite and rare-earth demand is also expected to grow strongly. Electric vehicles, energy storage, renewable generation and electricity grids remain major drivers. The expansion of data centres and other digital infrastructure adds another dimension to mineral requirements.
Copper Occupies a Distinct Position
Copper is central to power networks, electrical equipment and industrial systems. The IEA projects the largest absolute increase in demand for copper among the minerals assessed, adding approximately seven million tonnes by 2040. This does not imply that demand will rise in a straight line: economic growth, construction cycles and investment spending will still affect annual consumption. However, the long-term requirement for grid expansion makes copper supply planning strategically important.
More Projects Do Not Remove All Supply Risk
The pipeline of announced projects has improved the projected market balance for several minerals. The IEA estimates that the copper supply gap in its base case has narrowed from around 30% to 25%, while the outlook for lithium has also improved. These are projections, not confirmed future shortages. Mine approvals, financing, construction timelines and operating performance will determine how much planned capacity becomes actual production.
Processing Remains the Weak Link
New mining projects are being developed across a wider set of countries, but refining and downstream manufacturing remain concentrated. Rare earths illustrate the problem: announced mining capacity outside the leading producer exceeds the capacity planned for refining, separation and magnet manufacturing. Similar mismatches affect lithium and other battery materials. Without processing capacity, a country can mine ore yet remain dependent on overseas facilities to turn it into usable industrial inputs.
Industrial Policy Reshapes Investment Decisions
Governments are seeking to diversify mineral supplies for energy security, manufacturing and strategic industries. Support for domestic processing can encourage investment, but projects must still contend with high capital costs, skilled-labour requirements and competitive international markets. Export restrictions and production quotas can also change expected supply. The IEA notes that the projected cobalt supply gap has widened, reflecting developments in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
What the Next Decade Will Test
The challenge is to develop complete supply chains rather than isolated mining assets. Progress will depend on permitting, infrastructure, electricity costs, financing and the pace at which processing plants reach commercial operation. The balance between diversification and economic efficiency will shape how resilient the next generation of mineral supply networks becomes.
Critical minerals are becoming a strategic macroeconomic priority. Future resilience will depend as much on refining and manufacturing investment as on the volume of minerals identified underground.

India’s emerging industrial policy for critical minerals value chains entails more than a dozen regulatory, financial, and trade instruments worth nearly $40 billion, as part of a broader industrialization agenda.
The combination of three features distinguishes India’s critical minerals industrial strategy from other lower- and middle-income countries. First, the government is actively supporting multiple stages of the value chain, not only mining. Second, complementary policies, such as manufacturing incentives and consumer subsidies, stimulate domestic demand for critical minerals. Third, India is pursuing measures to secure mineral supplies from abroad, given its heavy import dependence.
But the success of India’s industrial policy will also depend on addressing transnational coordination challenges, both with mineral-rich developing economies seeking to build their own productive capabilities and with advanced economies furthering mineral security and manufacturing goals.
India could address these transnational challenges by positioning itself as a “third way” within the global critical minerals industrial ecosystem, distinct from both China’s state-capital-intensive model and Western security-led strategies. Drawing on its market scale, manufacturing capabilities, and engineering expertise, India could act as an industrial bridge that supports value addition in developing economies and diversification of critical mineral supply for advanced economies.
1. Introduction
India is rapidly developing a more coordinated industrial policy for critical minerals. In 2023, the Ministry of Mines identified 30 minerals as critical to the Indian economy based on their economic importance and supply risk.[i] The following year, the Union Budget proposed a Critical Minerals Mission among its manufacturing and services priorities for “Viksit Bharat”, India’s broader ambition to become a developed economy by 2047.[ii] The National Critical Mineral Mission (NCMM), followed in January 2025, establishing the government’s principal framework for securing critical mineral supplies and developing domestic capabilities across the value chain,[iii] with the stated objective of establishing a “globally competitive and resilient critical mineral ecosystem.”[iv]
Three features of India’s critical minerals strategy distinguish it from other low- and middle-income countries’ efforts. First, the government is intervening across multiple stages of the value chain rather than concentrating principally on mineral extraction. Second, these interventions are reinforced by policies outside the mining sector that stimulate domestic demand for mineral-intensive technologies, including manufacturing incentives for batteries, rare-earth magnets, solar photovoltaics, and semiconductors, as well as consumer subsidies for electric vehicles and rooftop solar. Third, India is simultaneously pursuing measures to secure mineral inputs from abroad.
Successfully implementing such an ambitious industrial policy is fraught with various fiscal, institutional, and technological challenges. But the need to secure imported inputs to feed a robust critical minerals industry—India depends on mineral resources, technologies, and finance from abroad—places a significant constraint on what domestic policy alone can accomplish.
The effectiveness of India’s critical minerals industrial policy, therefore, is contingent in large part on how it manages two transnational coordination complexities. The first concerns resource-rich producer countries that increasingly seek to expand their own processing, refining, and manufacturing capabilities rather than remain suppliers of raw materials. The second concerns India’s relationships with high-income partners whose interests in diversifying critical mineral supply chains align with India’s, but whose mineral security strategies increasingly favor stricter trade and investment regimes that retain manufacturing within their own economies.
This commentary first examines Indian policies for building out its critical minerals industry before assessing transnational constraints that would need to be addressed to reach its goals. The authors propose that India could articulate a clearer vision of itself as a “third way” within the global critical minerals industrial ecosystem that neither replicates China’s state-capital-intensive model nor simply integrates into Western security-led supply chains. In this role, India could function as an industrial bridge—using joint ventures, long-term offtake arrangements, technology and skills partnerships, and selective co-investment—to build mutually reinforcing value chains across low- and middle-income producer countries and advanced-economy partners.
2. Distinct Features of India’s Critical Minerals Industrial Policy
The NCMM is the organizing framework for India’s critical minerals industrial policy, but the strategy extends beyond the mission itself. In terms of budget, NCMM provides $1.7 billion (₹16,300 crore) in direct support and anticipates a further $1.88 billion (₹18,000 crore) in investments by public-sector undertakings (PSUs) through FY2030–31.[v] When combined with complementary policies by other ministries and departments, the announced financial outlays reach nearly $40 billion (see the appendix for a breakdown of policies). A review of government documents and announcements around these policies reveals three distinctive features of India’s strategy.
A Holistic Approach to Building Mineral Value Chains
First, India is intervening across multiple stages of the critical minerals value chain rather than focusing principally on extraction. The NCMM’s objectives encompass mineral exploration, mining, beneficiation, and recycling alongside technology development, skills, and financing.[vi] There are regulatory reforms to facilitate domestic exploration by opening up a formerly restricted group of commodities to private and foreign investment, the auctioning of exploration licenses, and the approval of 100 percent foreign direct investment (FDI) in exploration and mining activity. These are accompanied by fiscal measures for building various midstream capabilities, including support for domestic and international collaborative R&D, establishment of critical mineral processing parks, and funding a National Critical Minerals Stockpile for at least five commodities by 2031. The Science and Technology Programme for Promoting Research and Innovation in Startups and MSMEs (micro, small, and medium enterprises) (S&T PRISM) initiative pre-dates the NCMM, and funds start-ups working on commercializing technologies in mineral processing, metallurgy, and recycling. Finally, a set of regulations target the recovery of critical minerals from solar PV modules, batteries, and other electronics. Together, these interventions aim to create productive capabilities across upstream, midstream, and downstream segments of the mining value chain.
Complementary Policies to Spur Domestic Demand
India’s critical minerals strategy extends to industrial policy tools that generate domestic demand in industries that use minerals as inputs.
Manufacturing incentives through the Production Linked Incentive Scheme deliver payments tied to quantitative metrics for sales, outputs, and domestic value addition (DVA) requirements for firms. Three of the schemes outlined in the appendix are specific to critical minerals (advanced chemistry cells [ACC], sintered rare earth permanent magnets, and critical mineral recycling), whereas the other schemes target the downstream users of these commodities (solar PV and semiconductors). The ACC scheme, for example, provides $1.9 billion (₹18,100 crore) in incentives to establish large-scale domestic battery cell manufacturing and requires beneficiaries to achieve at least 25 percent domestic value addition, rising to 60 percent within five years.[vii]

Copper prices are set to stay near record highs next year as new mines struggle to keep pace with demand from power grids and data centres, the World Bank forecasts.
The bank raised its 2027 copper price estimate 18% from April to $13,000 per tonne, or about $5.90 per lb., in its October outlook, released Wednesday. That’s only 1.5% below the $13,200 average it now projects for this year.
“Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once,” Ayhan Kose, the bank’s deputy chief economist, said in a news release. “Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity and economic growth.”
For miners and investors, the outlook points to sustained demand for new copper supply alongside higher costs and an uneven recovery across other commodities. Electrification is supporting industrial metals, while weak construction weighs on iron ore and high silver prices encourage manufacturers to use less of it.
The bank expects its metals and minerals index, which includes base metals and iron ore but excludes precious metals, to rise 25% this year before easing 3.3% in 2027. Even after that decline, the index would stand 16% above its 2021 peak. The forecasts are calendar-year averages, based on information available through Oct. 14.
Supply limits
Long development timelines help explain why the bank expects prices to remain elevated. Investment is shifting toward industries that use more base metals, while exploration and mine construction can take more than a decade and refining capacity remains concentrated in a handful of countries.
Copper’s recent gains haven’t depended entirely on stronger consumption. Global demand slipped slightly in the first half, the bank found. Mine disruptions and the movement of refined metal into U.S. warehouses helped tighten availability elsewhere.
Uncertainty over possible U.S. import tariffs created a premium for copper traded on Comex over London Metal Exchange prices, drawing shipments toward the United States. That gap narrowed substantially by September, but uncertainty over tariffs taking effect in January could encourage further stockpiling and regional shortages.
Mine supply growth is expected to remain subdued as Indonesia deals with lingering weather-related disruptions and Chile faces operational constraints and declining grades. Demand should strengthen in 2027–28 through investment in electricity networks, data centres and electric vehicles.
Trade policy is adding another constraint. The Democratic Republic of Congo banned copper concentrate exports in August to encourage domestic processing, although exemptions could limit the immediate impact, the bank said. Its supporting data show 147 restrictive measures affecting critical minerals through September, against 63 measures easing trade. Those counts give every intervention equal weight, regardless of the volume of trade affected.
Uneven gains
The bank’s upward revisions extend beyond copper. It increased next year’s tin forecast 22% from April to $45,000 a tonne and its zinc estimate 13% to $3,100. Both metals are still expected to fall about 11%-12% from this year’s averages as supply improves.
Iron ore faces a different market. Weak Chinese construction and rising supply from established exporters and Guinea’s Simandou project are expected to keep pressure on prices. The bank retained its April forecast of $95 a dry tonne for 2027, down from $98 this year.
Nor does expanding clean-energy demand lift every battery material equally. Cobalt and lithium prices fell 25% and 13%, respectively, in the third quarter. Restarted Australian mines, resumed Zimbabwean concentrate exports and softer Chinese electric-vehicle sales momentum weighed on lithium.
Nickel faces competition from nickel-free lithium-iron-phosphate batteries. Stainless steel, which accounts for about two-thirds of nickel use, remains its main demand driver. The bank expects nickel prices to be little changed next year.
Precious pullback
Gold is forecast to average $4,250 per oz. in 2027, down 7.6% from this year’s projected $4,600. The bank trimmed next year’s estimate from $4,300 in April, expecting investment demand and central-bank buying to moderate while remaining supportive.
Those two sources accounted for about half of gold demand in the first half. Jewellery consumption has declined sharply since 2023, while high prices are encouraging recycling. Mine production is expected to increase only modestly.
Silver’s industrial exposure creates a sharper trade-off. The bank projects an average of $62 per oz. next year, down 11% from $70 this year and below April’s $65 forecast.
High prices are encouraging solar manufacturers to reduce silver use and substitute copper in the electrical contacts of photovoltaic cells. Growing consumption from electronics, data centres, vehicles and power infrastructure should partly offset those losses, but recycling and modest mine-supply gains are expected to ease market tightness.
Shared shocks
A companion study offers another caution for commodity investors: price volatility becomes more connected during periods of global stress.
Using daily data for 15 commodities from 2006 through June 2026, the bank found roughly one-third of volatility was associated with shocks in other commodity markets. About half of those connections occurred within broad commodity groups.
Industrial metals and food were the main net transmitters of volatility. Copper and silver stood out as bridges between markets, alongside oil and maize. These are statistical relationships; the model doesn’t establish that a shock in one market causes volatility in another.
Energy exposure
For producers, higher metal prices can come with more expensive fuel, power and processing inputs. The bank expects European electricity costs to continue constraining aluminum and zinc smelting, while disruption to Middle Eastern sulphur shipments could raise nickel-processing costs in Indonesia.
U.S. diesel prices reached record levels in October, the bank found. Damage to refineries in the Gulf region and Russia could keep diesel supplies tight even as crude exports recover, the bank said.
Its baseline assumes Brent crude eases to $79 a barrel next year from $91 in 2026. Even that lower forecast is 13% above April’s $70 estimate. An adverse scenario involving further energy-supply disruptions would put the 2027 average at $105.
Supply setbacks could therefore push metal prices above the forecasts while squeezing producers’ margins. If higher energy prices instead drive inflation, interest rates and financing costs high enough to weaken investment and manufacturing, the same shock could undermine industrial-metal demand.

articles.title: Cheniere Energy signs long-term LNG supply deal with QatarEnergy covering deliveries through 2054 - Energies Media
articles.summary: Cheniere Energy signs long-term LNG supply deal with QatarEnergy covering deliveries through 2054  Energies Media
articles.full_text:
Cheniere Energy just signed two long-term LNG supply agreements totaling up to 4 million metric tonnes per year (mtpa) with QatarEnergy. Deliveries will run from the early 2030s all the way through the end of 2054. Under the deal, Cheniere’s Sabine Pass and Corpus Christi subsidiaries will each supply 2 mtpa, with up to 1 million metric tonnes per year of the Sabine Pass portion dependent on a positive final investment decision on the first phase of the Sabine Pass Liquefaction Expansion Project.
Deal details: Volumes, timeline, and FID condition
The agreements cover both the Sabine Pass LNG terminal in Louisiana and the Corpus Christi LNG terminal in Texas. Deliveries start in the early 2030s and run straight through to the end of 2054 — more than two decades of continuous supply.
Up to 1 million metric tonnes per year (tpy) of that volume hinges on Cheniere reaching a positive final investment decision (FID) on the first phase of its Sabine Pass Liquefaction (SPL) Expansion Project. That condition matters because it ties a chunk of the deal directly to whether Cheniere moves ahead with new infrastructure — making this both a commercial contract and a statement of intent.
The volumes are split evenly at 2 mtpa from Sabine Pass and 2 mtpa from Corpus Christi on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, indexed to Henry Hub plus a fixed fee.
The volumes are split evenly at 2 mtpa from Sabine Pass and 2 mtpa from Corpus Christi on a free-on-board (FOB) basis, indexed to Henry Hub plus a fixed fee. Worth noting is the structure itself. Long-term LNG contracts running past 2050 are increasingly rare, and when two major players commit to one, it reflects genuine confidence in sustained natural gas demand over the coming decades.
Why the agreement was reached: Strategic drivers for both parties
For Cheniere, the logic is pretty straightforward. The company has consistently used long-term offtake agreements as the commercial foundation for its expansion projects. Without committed buyers willing to sign multi-decade contracts, securing financing and reaching FID on new liquefaction capacity gets considerably harder. This deal adds another anchor customer to the case for pushing the SPL Expansion forward.
QatarEnergy’s motivations run parallel but from a different direction. Qatar is one of the world’s largest LNG producers and has been aggressively diversifying its customer base for several years. Locking in long-term revenue streams across different geographies reduces exposure to any single market while reinforcing Qatar’s position as a reliable global supplier.
The broader market context matters here too. Global LNG demand has been climbing — driven by energy security concerns in Europe after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, continued growth in Asian markets, and a wider push to replace coal with gas in power generation. That rising demand has intensified competition for long-term supply contracts, pushing buyers and sellers to move fast and commit early.
Implications for Cheniere’s SPL expansion project and US LNG exports
This deal strengthens the commercial case for a positive FID on the first phase of the SPL Expansion. If approved, the expansion would add meaningful new liquefaction capacity at Sabine Pass — one of the busiest LNG export terminals in the US — and every long-term contract Cheniere signs brings that FID closer by demonstrating sustained buyer interest.
Should the expansion go ahead, it would boost US LNG export capacity at a moment when American LNG has become increasingly central to global energy markets. The US has grown into one of the world’s top LNG exporters in recent years, and projects like the SPL Expansion would extend that position well into the future.
The multi-decade length of this contract also carries implications beyond volumes. A deal running through 2054 gives QatarEnergy’s downstream customers a form of energy security, while handing Cheniere a predictable, long-horizon revenue base. In an industry where price volatility and geopolitical disruption are constant risks, that kind of stability has real value on both sides.
Background: Cheniere, QatarEnergy, and the global LNG landscape
Cheniere Energy is the largest LNG exporter in the United States, operating two major facilities: Sabine Pass in Louisiana and Corpus Christi in Texas. Sabine Pass was the first large-scale LNG export terminal to come online in the contiguous US and remains the country’s highest-capacity export site. Cheniere’s business model leans heavily on long-term contracts, which underpin project financing and support expansion decisions.
QatarEnergy sits at the other end of the spectrum. One of the largest LNG producers in the world, Qatar has been ramping up production capacity significantly, with ambitions to grow output from around 77 million tpy to 142 million tpy by 2030. Placing that volume has required a wave of long-term supply agreements with buyers across Europe, Asia, and the Americas.
The broader trend toward long-term LNG contracting has been one of the defining features of the global gas market since 2022. Buyers who once preferred shorter, more flexible deals shifted course after supply disruptions exposed the risks of leaning too heavily on spot markets. Major deals involving suppliers from the US, Qatar, Australia, and elsewhere have been announced steadily through 2023, 2024, and into 2025.
What this deal means in summary
The Cheniere-QatarEnergy agreement is a clear example of how the LNG market has repositioned itself around long-term commitments. For Cheniere Energy, the 4 mtpa commitment across its two flagship facilities adds commercial weight to the SPL Expansion Project and reinforces a strategy built on stable, contracted revenue. For QatarEnergy, it secures another long-term outlet as production scales up. For the wider market, it’s one more data point confirming that buyers and sellers alike are betting on natural gas staying central to the global energy mix well into the 2050s.

articles.summary: Glencore, CNGR back $380M Brazil nickel mine with $40M  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Glencore (LON: GLEN) and China’s CNGR have committed $40 million to Centaurus Metals (ASX: CTM) and agreed to buy the entire forecast nickel concentrate output from its $380 million Jaguar project in Brazil for its first five years of operations, bringing the mine closer to a final investment decision.
The two companies will each invest $20 million in Centaurus and purchase at least 20,000 dry metric tonnes of nickel concentrate annually under separate five-year agreements starting in the first half of 2029, the Australian miner said Wednesday. The contracts cover material containing 30% nickel, with an estimated combined net sales value of $900 million at current metal prices.
“With 100% of Jaguar’s forecast output over the first five years now contracted and $40 million of new strategic equity committed, we have significantly advanced both the commercial and funding foundations to develop the project,” Centaurus managing director Darren Gordon said in a statement.
The agreements strengthen Jaguar’s prospects as Brazil seeks to expand its role in supplying battery metals to global markets. They also underscore the willingness of major commodity traders and Chinese battery-materials manufacturers to secure long-term nickel supplies, even as developers face substantial financing requirements and volatile metal prices.
Financing momentum
Centaurus said its senior debt financing process is well advanced, with the new equity commitments helping it complete the funding package required to authorize construction at Jaguar, in Pará state.
The investment will be made in two tranches, with Glencore and CNGR initially contributing $12.5 million each. A second payment of $7.5 million from each company depends on shareholder approval and a final investment decision. CNGR’s participation also requires Chinese outbound investment approval, with conditions for the second tranche subject to a Jan. 31, 2027 deadline.
Both investors will receive shares priced at A$0.425 apiece, a 5% premium to Centaurus’ 20-day volume-weighted average share price before the agreements were signed.
The new purchase commitments build on an existing Glencore contract announced in March. Together, the arrangements cover approximately 22,500 tonnes of contained nickel annually during Jaguar’s initial five years of production.
Prices will be linked to the London Metal Exchange cash settlement nickel price, with the proportion of metal value paid to Centaurus varying according to market conditions. The contracts also provide payments for copper and cobalt byproducts.
The buyers can terminate their agreements if Centaurus fails to ship the first nickel concentrate by the end of 2029, leaving the developer facing a firm commercial deadline as it works to secure financing and begin construction.
Nickel pipeline
Brazil’s nickel industry is attracting growing investment interest as mining companies position themselves to supply metals used in electric vehicles, batteries and other industrial applications.
The Brazilian Mining Institute (Ibram) expects nickel projects to attract $4.7 billion between 2026 and 2030, up 24.2% from its previous five-year investment forecast.
The outlook comes amid expectations of stronger long-term demand from electrification and potential supply constraints following production cuts in Indonesia, the world’s dominant nickel producer. However, the sector remains exposed to price volatility and competition from lower-cost Indonesian operations.
Vale (NYSE: VALE), one of the world’s largest mining companies, has said its copper and nickel businesses could contribute about 40% of its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization in the coming years, reflecting the growing importance of base metals to its portfolio.
Other developers are advancing Brazilian nickel investments. In July, Brazilian Nickel secured support from the Brazilian National Development Bank for its $1.4-billion Piauí project.
MMG Singapore Resources has been less successful. The subsidiary of Chinese state-owned MMG is seeking to resolve European Commission objections to its proposed $500-million acquisition of Anglo American’s (LON: AAL) nickel assets in Brazil.
