articles.title: Rio Tinto pumps $1.4 billion into lithium projects in Argentina - Mining.com
articles.summary: Rio Tinto pumps $1.4 billion into lithium projects in Argentina  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Rio Tinto (ASX, LON: RIO) is doubling down on Argentina’s lithium market with the opening of two projects backed by a combined $1.4-billion investment, boosting its production capacity as the mining giant pursues ambitious global growth in battery metals.
The Fénix 1B expansion and Sal de Vida operation in Catamarca province both achieved first production in the second quarter of 2026, ahead of schedule, and are now ramping up output. Together, they will add 25,000 tonnes of annual lithium carbonate equivalent (LCE) capacity once fully operational, the company said.
“These two projects build on nearly three decades of lithium production in Catamarca and the expertise of our Argentine workforce,” Rio Tinto CEO Simon Trott said at an inauguration ceremony attended by President Javier Milei and Catamarca Governor Raúl Jalil. “They demonstrate our industry-leading project delivery capability, as we execute with discipline towards our global target of 200,000 tonnes lithium carbonate equivalent annual production capacity by 2028.”
The investment strengthens Argentina’s position as an emerging lithium powerhouse at a time when demand for the battery-making mineral is expected to accelerate. The country is forecast to produce about 172,700 tonnes of LCE in 2026, up 48% from last year and more than five times its 2018 output.
The expansion also comes as producers face pressure to control costs and demonstrate the commercial viability of newer extraction technologies amid volatile lithium prices.
Expanding production
The $530-million Fénix 1B expansion adds 10,000 tonnes of annual LCE capacity, increasing the operation’s total target to approximately 40,000 tonnes.
Rio Tinto is also evaluating a further expansion at Fénix that would require about $1 billion in additional investment. The proposed Fénix II lithium plant, also planned for the Hombre Muerto salt flat, could receive a final investment decision toward the end of the decade, Trott said.
“It’s under consideration; it would be the next phase of expansion,” Trott said during his visit to Argentina.
The company plans to submit Fénix II to Argentina’s RIGI in 2027, potentially securing long-term tax and regulatory benefits for the development.
Fénix began production in 1997 as Argentina’s first commercial lithium operation. Rio Tinto is already considering another expansion, with an investment decision expected in 2028 or 2029.
Sal de Vida, a new lithium carbonate operation about 20 km northeast of Fénix, has a target capacity of 15,000 tonnes annually. Its first phase involved an investment of $374 million.
The projects form part of Rio Tinto’s integrated production hub in the Salar del Hombre Muerto, which holds a combined resource base of approximately 19 million tonnes of LCE.
Managing the operations together allows the company to share infrastructure, improve efficiencies and pursue opportunities to reduce water consumption.
Fénix uses direct lithium extraction (DLE), while Sal de Vida relies on conventional evaporation ponds. DLE can substantially shorten processing times by separating lithium from brine without relying on prolonged solar evaporation.
Rio Tinto is positioning itself among the first major miners to build a large-scale lithium business around DLE, although questions remain about its costs, scalability and long-term performance.
French miner Eramet (EPA: ERA) has also deployed the technology at its Centenario Ratones project in Salta province, where production began in late 2024.
Including Fénix, Sal de Vida and Olaroz, Rio Tinto’s nominal lithium capacity in Argentina reaches approximately 100,000 tonnes of LCE annually.
Its broader Argentinean portfolio includes a 66.5% stake in Olaroz and its full ownership of the Rincón project, spanning the provinces of Catamarca, Jujuy and Salta.
Rio is also exploring opportunities to advance copper projects in the country, but Trott said the company’s immediate priority is to safely increase production and deliver reliable, high-quality lithium to customers while generating long-term returns.
Investment incentives
The inauguration brought together national and provincial officials, employees, suppliers and representatives of local and Indigenous communities, highlighting the political and economic importance of lithium development in Argentina.
“The expansion of the Fénix project is a historic milestone that demonstrates the potential of Argentina’s mining sector,” Milei said. “This was made possible by the country once again creating incentives for the production of resources that are essential to the modern world.”
Rio Tinto expects to spend nearly 70% of its planned $4 billion in Argentinean lithium growth capital with local suppliers, potentially strengthening regional supply chains and creating opportunities for domestic businesses.
The investment aligns with Milei’s efforts to attract foreign capital through market-oriented reforms and the Large Investment Incentive Regime (RIGI), which offers tax, legal and foreign-exchange benefits for 30 years to qualifying projects worth more than $200 million.
Lithium is becoming an increasingly important contributor to Argentina’s mining exports. Shipments of the mineral generated $1.467 billion between January and August 2026, a 190.5% increase from the same period a year earlier.
Argentina forms part of South America’s Lithium Triangle alongside Bolivia and Chile, a region estimated to hold about 60% of the world’s lithium reserves. The concentration of resources has attracted international miners seeking to secure long-term supplies for electric-vehicle batteries.
Long-term demand projections are encouraging further development. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence expects global lithium demand to rise from 2 million tonnes of LCE in 2026 to 7 million tonnes by 2050, driven largely by electric vehicles and energy storage.
Argentina’s Mining Secretariat forecasts the country could overtake Chile in lithium production by 2029 and reach annual output of 573,000 tonnes of LCE by 2035.
Reaching those levels will depend on sustained investment, successful project commissioning and producers’ ability to remain competitive through commodity price cycles.

articles.title: Nickel Institute defends nickel demand as INSG forecasts a market surplus - energynews.pro
articles.summary: Nickel Institute defends nickel demand as INSG forecasts a market surplus  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Veronique Steukers, president of the Nickel Institute, the global association of major primary nickel producers, describes durably supported demand in an interview with Platts, the price assessment agency of S&P Global, dated October 21, 2026. According to her, stainless steel remains the leading end use, joined by batteries, energy storage for data centers and defense. Her remarks come a few days after the autumn meeting of the International Nickel Study Group (INSG), an intergovernmental organization based in Lisbon. The group nonetheless forecasts a surplus market.
Rising consumption, but a reversed market balance
The INSG confirms a marked increase in global primary nickel consumption this year, followed by more moderate growth next year. On production, the president's reading is accurate: global primary nickel output remains nearly flat this year, before a sharp increase next year. Battery storage continues to attract financing, as shown by Delta Capacity reaching financial close on two 250 MW battery projects, while TotalEnergies subsidiary Saft launches solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux.
What the interview leaves in the background is the reversal of the market balance. In spring, the INSG forecast a deficit for this year, which would have been the first in several years. It now forecasts a slight surplus, which widens next year. The mechanism lies in the size of the revisions: the organization raised its production forecast more than its consumption forecast, and production growth exceeds consumption growth next year. Last year's surplus has itself been revised upward with each publication.
Batteries and Indonesian quotas: two points of tension
On batteries, the INSG is more cautious than the interview. It notes that nickel's share is growing more slowly than expected against nickel-free lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, and that global electric vehicle sales are growing only modestly this year, with a recovery expected next year. The president acknowledges a "softer" growth in demand for nickel batteries.
Indonesia is by far the world's leading mining producer. Jakarta steers supply through annual ore extraction quotas known as RKAB (Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya), a work plan and budget that each miner has approved by the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM). This year's quota had been set well below last year's. The government is now nonetheless easing its quotas.
Two readings of the market
RKAB quotas are expressed in tonnes of wet ore, not in contained nickel. They therefore cannot be directly compared with the INSG's figures, which cover primary nickel.
The Nickel Institute highlights demand supported by stainless steel, batteries, data centers and defense. The INSG, for its part, projects a surplus market this year and next, with production growing faster than consumption.

articles.title: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas - Mining.com
articles.summary: Glencore cobalt output sinks 52% under DRC quotas  Mining.com
articles.full_text:
Glencore (LON: GLEN), one of the world’s largest cobalt producers, reported a 52% drop in output during the first nine months of 2026 as export quotas in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) prompted it to leave more of the battery metal unprocessed.
The Swiss-based miner produced 13,700 tonnes of its own-sourced cobalt through September, down from 28,500 tonnes a year earlier, according to its third-quarter production report released Thursday. Output fell 20% quarter-on-quarter to 3,500 tonnes.
Glencore said it is increasingly retaining cobalt contained in mixed ore in solution rather than converting it into saleable hydroxide, cutting near-term processing costs. The company expects to recover the metal’s value as export regulations evolve, but excludes the retained material from reported production.
The strategy illustrates how the DRC’s efforts to control cobalt supply are changing mining operations, with companies delaying processing rather than producing material they cannot immediately export. It also raises the prospect of additional supply entering the market once restrictions ease.
Cobalt restrictions
The DRC, the world’s dominant cobalt-producing country, suspended exports in 2025 after prices slumped to nine-year lows. Authorities subsequently introduced quotas aimed at supporting prices, with restrictions expected to remain in place until at least the end of 2027.
Glencore said its Kamoto Copper Company (KCC) and Mutanda operations hold enough cobalt stocks to meet near-term export allocations. Its African Copper division, which includes the Congolese mines, produced 11,600 tonnes of cobalt through September, down 56% year-on-year.
The volume of cobalt being held in solution remains undisclosed, making it difficult to assess how much additional supply could eventually reach the market.
Copper operations, meanwhile, delivered stronger results. Glencore’s own-sourced production rose 3% to 598,600 tonnes from 583,500 tonnes a year earlier. Excluding the closure of Mount Isa’s copper mine and the sale of Kidd, output increased 12% on a comparable basis.
Higher mining rates and improved grades at African Copper, together with richer ore at Peru’s Antamina mine, offset weaker production at Antapaccay and Collahuasi.
Glencore aims to produce 1.6 million tonnes of copper annually by 2035, nearly double its current level, as it pursues demand from electrification, power grids and artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Production outlook
The company maintained its 2026 copper guidance of 810,000 to 870,000 tonnes, although it expects to finish near the bottom of that range. Steelmaking coal output is also tracking toward the lower end of its 30 million to 32 million-tonne target, while zinc and energy coal are expected near the upper ends of their forecasts.
“We are pleased to report a strong third quarter production performance, where our key assets largely performed in line with expectations and previously communicated guidance,” CEO Gary Nagle said.
BMO Capital Markets analyst Alexander Pearce said in a note the company’s quarterly production was slightly below expectations overall. Copper and steelmaking coal missed estimates by 3% and 7%, respectively, while zinc and thermal coal exceeded forecasts by 4% and 5%.
Pearce noted Glencore’s full-year outlook remained broadly consistent with BMO’s forecasts, indicating that the quarterly shortfalls could be offset during the final three months of 2026.
Steelmaking coal production declined 13% to 21.5 million tonnes through September because of lower plant throughput and yields at its EVR operations. Energy coal output edged up to 73.9 million tonnes from 73.5 million tonnes a year earlier.
Glencore also advanced the restart of its ferrochrome smelters, bringing Boshoek back online in September and Wonderkop in October, following the earlier restart of Lion. Attributable ferrochrome production climbed 29% from the second quarter.
The company reiterated its forecast for full-year marketing, adjusted earnings before interest and taxes to exceed $5 billion.

articles.title: Green Hydrogen Mission: How India plans to produce 5 million tonnes annually by 2030, transform its clean energy sector - Organiser
articles.summary: Green Hydrogen Mission: How India plans to produce 5 million tonnes annually by 2030, transform its clean energy sector  Organiser
articles.full_text:
India is expanding its clean energy ambitions beyond solar and wind power, with green hydrogen emerging as a potential solution for industries that are difficult to decarbonise. The government is developing a domestic ecosystem covering hydrogen production, electrolyser manufacturing, storage, transportation, industrial applications and exports.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM), approved by the Union Cabinet in January 2023 with an outlay of Rs 19,744 crore, is the central initiative driving this effort. It aims to establish India as a global hub for green hydrogen and its derivatives, including green ammonia and green methanol.
The mission targets at least five million metric tonnes of annual green hydrogen production capacity by 2030. If export demand develops as anticipated, India’s production potential could reach 10 million metric tonnes annually.
The initiative is also linked to India’s broader energy security objectives and its commitment to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2070. However, achieving these goals will depend on reducing production costs, expanding renewable electricity capacity, developing supporting infrastructure and creating a dependable market for green hydrogen.
What is Green Hydrogen?
Hydrogen is an energy carrier that can store and deliver energy for industrial processes, electricity generation and transportation. Unlike coal, petroleum and natural gas, hydrogen does not release carbon dioxide when used in a fuel cell. However, its overall environmental impact depends largely on how it is produced.
Most conventional hydrogen production relies on fossil fuels, particularly natural gas and coal. These methods can generate substantial carbon emissions. Green hydrogen offers an alternative by using renewable electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
The process is known as electrolysis. When electricity generated from solar, wind or other qualifying renewable sources powers an electrolyser, the resulting hydrogen can be produced with substantially lower emissions than conventional fossil-fuel-based hydrogen.
India’s abundant solar and wind resources provide an opportunity to produce hydrogen domestically. This could help the country reduce its reliance on imported fossil fuels while supplying industries that currently depend on hydrogen produced from natural gas.
Green hydrogen is particularly important for sectors where replacing fossil fuels with direct electrification is difficult. These include steel manufacturing, fertiliser production, petroleum refining, shipping and certain forms of heavy-duty transport.
Its development could also create opportunities in renewable energy, industrial equipment manufacturing, engineering, logistics, research and technology services.
How is Green Hydrogen produced?
Green hydrogen is primarily produced through water electrolysis, a process in which an electrolyser uses electricity to separate water into hydrogen and oxygen.
The process involves several stages.
1. Water purification: Water is treated to remove impurities that could damage the electrolyser or reduce its efficiency. According to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), approximately nine litres of demineralised water are required to produce one kilogram of hydrogen.
2. Renewable electricity generation: Solar or wind power supplies the electricity needed for electrolysis. The availability and cost of renewable electricity are among the most important factors affecting the overall cost of green hydrogen.
3. Electrolysis: Inside the electrolyser, electricity drives a chemical reaction that separates water into hydrogen and oxygen. The gases are collected separately.
4. Purification and compression: The hydrogen is dried and purified to meet the requirements of its intended application. It may then be compressed or converted into another chemical compound for storage, transportation or industrial use.
5. End-use application: The hydrogen can be used directly in industrial processes, supplied to fuel cells or converted into derivatives such as ammonia and methanol.
Different electrolyser technologies are available, including alkaline, proton exchange membrane and solid oxide systems. Each has different operating characteristics, costs and efficiency considerations.
Developing domestic manufacturing capacity for electrolysers is therefore an important part of India’s strategy. It could reduce dependence on imported equipment and help establish a domestic supply chain for the emerging industry.
What makes Hydrogen ‘Green’?
Hydrogen itself is a colourless gas. Terms such as green, grey and blue hydrogen are used to distinguish production methods and their associated emissions.
Grey hydrogen is generally produced from natural gas without capturing the resulting carbon emissions. Blue hydrogen also uses fossil fuels but incorporates carbon capture and storage. Green hydrogen uses renewable electricity for electrolysis.
The distinction matters because hydrogen can have a significant carbon footprint if its production depends on fossil fuels.
In August 2023, India notified its Green Hydrogen Standard. Under this standard, hydrogen qualifies as green when its emissions do not exceed two kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilogram of hydrogen, measured on a well-to-gate basis and averaged over 12 months.
The benchmark provides a common framework for assessing production-related emissions. India has also introduced standards for green ammonia and green methanol and established the Green Hydrogen Certification Scheme of India to support monitoring, verification and certification.
Such standards are important for domestic regulation and international trade. Potential buyers need reliable information about the emissions associated with the hydrogen and its derivatives before treating them as low-emission products.
Certification can also help ensure that claims about environmental benefits are supported by measurable data.
Where can Green Hydrogen be used?
Green hydrogen’s strongest near-term potential lies in industries that already consume hydrogen or require energy-intensive chemical and industrial processes. Replacing existing fossil-fuel-based hydrogen in these sectors may be more practical than immediately introducing hydrogen into every part of the economy.
1. Fertiliser production
Hydrogen is an essential input in ammonia production. Ammonia, in turn, is used extensively in the manufacture of nitrogen-based fertilisers.
Conventional ammonia production relies heavily on hydrogen derived from natural gas. Replacing this hydrogen with green hydrogen could reduce emissions from fertiliser manufacturing.
India has a large fertiliser industry and significant requirements for agricultural inputs. Green hydrogen could therefore help reduce industrial emissions while supporting the development of domestic clean-energy technologies. However, the cost of green hydrogen remains an important consideration because it affects the final cost of ammonia and fertilisers.
2. Petroleum refining
Refineries use hydrogen for several processes, including removing sulphur from petroleum products and upgrading heavier oil into fuels such as diesel, aviation turbine fuel and naphtha.
Much of the hydrogen used in conventional refining is produced from fossil fuels. Introducing green hydrogen could reduce emissions associated with these operations.
Refineries are potential early customers because they already have hydrogen-handling systems and established industrial demand. This may make the transition more practical than developing entirely new applications.
The extent of adoption will depend on production costs, supply reliability and the availability of renewable electricity.
3. Steel manufacturing
Steel production is another major opportunity for green hydrogen.
Traditional blast furnace-based steelmaking relies on coal and coke for heat and chemical reduction. These processes generate substantial carbon emissions.
Hydrogen can replace carbon-based reducing agents in certain direct reduced iron processes. When produced using renewable electricity, it offers a potential pathway towards lower-emission steel production.
India’s steel sector is expanding alongside infrastructure development, construction and manufacturing. Integrating green hydrogen could help reduce the emissions associated with future industrial growth.
However, hydrogen-based steelmaking requires significant investment in equipment, renewable power and supporting infrastructure. Pilot projects are therefore important for testing technical feasibility and commercial viability.
4. Heavy-duty road and rail transport
Hydrogen fuel cells convert hydrogen into electricity, which can power electric motors. These systems produce water and heat during operation.
Fuel-cell vehicles may be suitable for certain applications involving heavy loads, long operating ranges or limited time for recharging. Potential uses include buses, trucks and some railway applications.
However, hydrogen vehicles face competition from battery-electric alternatives. Their commercial prospects depend on vehicle costs, fuel prices, refuelling infrastructure, operational requirements and the availability of reliable hydrogen supplies.
India is supporting pilot projects to test hydrogen-powered mobility and assess where the technology may offer practical advantages.
5. Shipping and port operations
Shipping is exploring alternative fuels to reduce emissions from conventional marine fuels. Green hydrogen can be converted into green ammonia or green methanol, both of which are being considered for certain maritime applications.
Ports could play an important role by providing storage, handling, bunkering and refuelling facilities.
India’s major ports may also become locations for hydrogen production and export infrastructure because they connect industrial consumers, renewable energy projects and international shipping routes.

New Delhi: The World Bank projected energy prices to increase 32% in 2026, reversing three years of declines. However, the financial institution is hopeful about prices moderating in 2027.
Brent, which has recorded a huge surge in prices, due to the US-Iran war, is expected to average $91 per barrel in 2026, up from $69 in 2025, then ease to $79 in 2027.
World Bank Sees Copper Prices Staying Near Record Highs
Copper prices will stay near record highs next year as new mines struggle to meet demand from power grids and data centres, according to World Bank forecasts.
The bank raised its 2027 copper estimate 18% from April to $13,000 per tonne, or about $5.90 per lb. Additional revisions include raising next year's tin forecast 22% to $45,000 a tonne and the zinc estimate 13% to $3,100. Conversely, gold is expected to average $4,250 per oz. in 2027, which is a 7.6% decline from this year.
“Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once,” Ayhan Kose, World Bank’s deputy chief economist, said.
“Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity and economic growth,” Kose added.
Food Prices To Rise
The World Bank in its October report projected food commodity prices to rise about 10% in 2026 and another 7% in 2027. It attributed the possibility of high prices to grain shipment disruption due to the Middle East crisis, El Niño impact, and high fuel and fertiliser prices. Overall commodity prices are forecast to rise 23% this year before declining by 7% in 2027.
The Middle East conflict has forced the countries to make adjustments on production and consumption of energy. The WB estimates global oil supply to slump 5.2% in 2026—the largest drop in more than four decades outside the 2020 global recession. “Consumption is expected to decline 2.5%, the third-largest annual contraction on record, after 2020 and 1980. High prices amid supply shortages are curbing demand, while electrification is also reducing oil use, particularly in China. Even so, production remains below consumption, forcing further withdrawals from oil stocks and leaving markets more exposed to renewed disruption,” the report stated.
Fertiliser prices
Fertiliser prices are projected to increase 14% in 2026, after a surge in urea prices early in the year that has since eased, before returning to 2025 levels in 2027.
The World Bank finds links between commodity-price volatility become more pronounced during periods of economic or market stress, including since the start of the current conflict in the Middle East.

articles.title: Corn farmers adapt to climate change - The Alpena News
articles.summary: Corn farmers adapt to climate change  The Alpena News
articles.full_text:
LANSING -- As climate change strongly affects agriculture, rising temperatures are pushing corn farmers to adopt different management practices to protect their crop yields.
"Climatologists forecast less frequent but more intense rain events, leading to increased likelihood of temporary drought and/or excess moisture conditions," according to a recent study by researchers at Michigan State University and the University of Illinois.
"Irrigation and drought-tolerant seed varieties can reduce the risk of yield loss to drought, while drainage can reduce the risk of yield loss to puddling and excess water," the study said.
The top five producing counties for corn are Lenawee, Sanilac, Saginaw, Gratiot and Tuscola, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.
The study in the journal Ecological Economics was based on interviews with 44 Michigan corn farmers.
Researchers Natalie Loduca and Scott Swinton wrote that the findings have implications for outreach and Extension activities.
"Extension programs that target climate adaptation technologies may be more effective when they put primary emphasis on productivity benefits ahead of risk-management ones," the study said.
Kristin Poley, the director of research for the Corn Marketing Program of Michigan, said, "Michigan corn farmers are adopting management practices that improve soil health, such as cover crops, or water management, such as tile or controlled drainage, to mitigate risks.
"Irrigation was perceived as providing both yield and risk benefits, whereas tile draining drainage and drought-resistant seeds were viewed primarily as risk-reducing technologies," Poley said.
Increased changes in weather patterns, she said, "make corn production difficult due to unpredictable growing conditions year-to-year."
She said examples of weather changes include "wet spring delaying planting, hot dry summer stressors that leave crops vulnerable to diseases, as well as excessive rainfall during mid-seasons, which can restrict root development and increase nutrient loss."
Those variables make it difficult for farmers to plan and respond to the uncertainties that affect increased production costs, labor availability and nutrient management. That creates a gap in farm profitability, according to Poley.
She said the financial challenges that Michigan corn farmers face include the cost of fertilizer, seed and crop protection products. Those are caused by unpredictable weather conditions that damage crops or reduce future yields and profit margins.
Soil is also affected by changes in climate. Poley said, "Michigan has a large variety of soil types. Depending on weather conditions, the soil types can be strongly influenced, such as poorly drained soils that lead to water and nutrient loss."
Looking ahead to long-term economic consequences that Michigan corn farmers could face if the current climate trends continue, they include "greater financial volatility, increased pressure on soil and water resources, and more complex pest and disease management," Poley said.
Lastly, Poley said, "The risk is not simply that Michigan will produce less corn every year. It is that maintaining consistent yields and profitable production will require more investment and more adaptive management."
